Grijalva>: The College Fix's analysis is plagued by many of the same assumptions made by AEI. In many of the years of its decades of analysis, the number of scholars whose politics could not be determined was greater than the number of liberal and conservative coded scholars combined.\26\ While they claimed to see liberal scholars everywhere, the College Fix also seemed to go out of its way to deny that conservative scholars existed. In describing one member of the 2021 cohort, they said, ``One of the award winners, an economics student at Michigan State, interned at the conservative American Enterprise Institute and interned with the White House Council of Economic Advisors during the Donald Trump administration, but his political affiliation remains unclear.''\27\ In 2022, a year the website said the Truman cohort was ``dominated'' by Democrats and progressives, 5 scholars had worked in Democratic offices, 3 had worked in Republican offices.\28\

The Majority's oversight of the Truman Foundation is a continuation of its narrative alleging there is a conservative bias on campus. They claim the lack of ``viewpoint diversity'' on campus inhibits the ability of conservative students to express their views. Evidence suggests that notwithstanding such a viewpoint imbalance, conservative thought continues to flourish on college campuses. The Majority's analysis consistently fails to acknowledge that conservative speech on campus is propped up by a vast network of outside organizations that support such speech,

By their own accounts, there are over 2,000 College Republicans chapters on American college campuses,\30\ over 2,000 chapters of Young Americans for Freedom,\31\ over 800 college chapters of Turning Point USA,\32\ and over 200 chapters of the Federalist Society at U.S. law schools.\33\ This is just the most public tip of the iceberg of infrastructure and private capital dedicated to incubating conservative thinkers and leaders on campus and vaulting them into positions of political influence in Washington, D.C. and state capitals around the country.\34\ Claims of a campus free speech crisis simply perpetuate the need to continue to subsidize more conservative voices on campus who then claim as part of their activism, that there is a free speech crisis on campus.\35\

Further, the Committee's Oversight of the Truman Foundation relies heavily on the purported ability to ``code'' certain topics of study as ``conservative'' or ``liberal''. This approach assumes the rhetorical lines politicians use to debate issues in Washington are transferrable to the academic disciplines researchers work in. In many instances, that is simply not the case. There is ``unequivocal'' scientific data that show global surface temperatures have been rising since the mid 1970s.\36\ Similarly there is a near universal consensus among climate scientists that human activity is largely responsible for driving this rise.\37\ So for highly motivated postgraduate scientists looking to continue research in their field towards the end of public service, i.e. Truman Scholars, climate change is likely not a political debate between conservatives and liberals, but instead an established problem that needs addressing by our best and brightest minds, their political beliefs notwithstanding.\38\

H.R. 7894 INFUSES POLITICS INTO THE TRUMAN SCHOLARSHIP
After decrying the problem of the politicization of the Truman Scholarship, H.R. 7894 makes significant changes throughout Truman Scholarship's authorizing statute that will infuse more politics into the program. Section 2 of H.R. 7894 creates a definition of ``affiliated with'' to refine requirements in current law that certain members of the Scholarship's Board of Trustees be ``from each political party''.\39\ The bill also inserts political party affiliation requirements into the Regional Review Panels, the bodies that interview all finalists for the scholarship and recommend candidates from each state to be scholars to the Foundation.\40\ The ideological background of members of these review panels was an issue that the Majority raised in hearing, despite the fact that the Scholarship's regulations state that a panels' recommendations are based on the Finalist's application, and their evaluation of the Finalist's ``leadership potential and communication skills, likelihood of ``making a difference'' in public service, and intellectual strength, analytical abilities, and prospects of performing well in graduate school''.\41\ By intentionally politicizing the panels, it will call into question whether scholars are selected per the regulations, or selected for their politics.

Section 3 of the bill changes the statutory composition of the Foundation's Board of Trustees. Some of these changes are cosmetic, others are not. For example, eight of the 13 Board members would still be nominated by the President, and require Senate confirmation; the Secretary of Education, or her designee would still serve ex officio. However, the bill re-words the requirements for the four Congressionally-appointed members of the Board. Under current law, the House and Senate-appointed members of the Board are Members of the House and Senate respectively. Under H.R. 7894, the Congressionally-appointed Board members are just nominated by the Speaker and Minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate--there is no requirement the nominees are Members of the House or Senate. In further revisions, Board members would now be term limited to two six-year terms and the bill enshrines that seven members of the Board shall constitute a quorum. The bill then mandates that within 90 days of the date of enactment of the Act (in this case the date of President's signature), the entire current Board would be dissolved and current Members terminated. This would allow President Trump to immediately appoint eight new members to the Board. While the bill does provide those appointments to be staggered--only two of the eight Presidential appointments to the new Board will serve six year terms--it would vest quorum proof control of the Board in the hands of Trump appointed nominees for two years.
